codebook.source: MONK-2 problem (Thrun et al. 1991), PMLB 'monk2' deduplicated to the 432 input configurations; attributes a1-a6 are abstract (no real-world meaning), so statements are phrased in rule terms on the attribute values

ann_25.text: This part of the model acts on 95 of the 345 training cases, and 6 of those 95 are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 3, a3 = 2, a4 = 2, a5 = 4, a6 = 2), it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.

For the typical case with a6 = 2, moving a5 away from its first value, or changing a1 from 1 to 2, clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 2% to about 99%, while with a6 = 1 it stays below 1%.
For the typical case with a5 other than 1, changing a1 from 1 to 2 clearly raises it from below 1% to about 81%, while with a5 = 1 it stays below 1%.

Through this part, for the typical case it acts on, moving a1, a3, a5 or a6 away from its first value slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' (a5 from about 1% to below 1%), and giving a2 or a4 its first value, or changing a2 from 3 to 2, slightly raises it.
The effect of a1 through this part is also slightly larger when a2 = 3 than when a2 = 1.

ann_26.text: Through this part, moving a1, a3, a5 or a6 away from its first value slightly raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' (a6 from below 1% to about 2%), and giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly lowers it.
Changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises it, so this part also separates a2 = 2 from a2 = 3.

ann_27.text: For the typical case, changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes', which stays below 1%.
So the model as a whole treats a2 = 2 and a2 = 3, two values other than the first, slightly differently.

ann_25.original: A fewer-than-two-indicators gate. Write I_k = 1 when attribute k takes its first value (a3:2 = 1-I3 and a6:2 = 1-I6, since a3 and a6 are binary). In these terms node 217 computes ReLU(13.02 - 8.77 I1 - 7.32 I2 - 6.57 I3 - 6.43 I4 - 9.36 I5 - 7.15 I6 - 0.20[a1=3] + 0.39[a2=3]), a near-uniform weighted count of active indicators (weights 6.4 to 9.4) subtracted from 13. It outputs about 13 when no indicator is active, 3.5 to 7.0 when exactly one is, and zero once two or more are. The one leak: the lightest pair (I3+I4) leaves at most +0.41, so the gate fires weakly on 6% of count-2 configurations. Evidence (train, n=345): node 217 ranges 12.82-13.40 at count 0, 3.46-6.98 at count 1, 0-0.41 at count 2, and exactly 0 at count>=3; sensitivities are about 0.8-1.15 for the six indicator columns and about 0.03-0.05 for a1:3 and a2:3, which are negligible.
ann_25.proposed: This part acts on 95 training cases, 6 of them actually 'yes', and pushes their predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% to below 1%; with it, moving a5 or a1 away from its first value turns the typical case with a6 = 2 to 'yes', and so does changing a1 from 1 to 2 when a5 is other than 1.

ann_26.original: A descending linear count ramp. The direct input-to-output connections sum, in rule-indicator terms, to 20.80 - 8.72 I1 - 9.45 I2 - 5.25 I3 - 10.01 I4 - 9.04 I5 - 11.95 I6 - 0.53[a1=2] - 0.45[a2=3]. a3 and a6 enter through both of their one-hot columns, which combine into single indicator weights. Each active indicator subtracts 5 to 12, and the weights are not uniform: I6 is heaviest (11.95) and I3 lightest (5.25). With the output bias (-1.20) the ramp is +18.6 to +19.6 at count 0, +6.7 to +14.4 at count 1, -3.3 to +5.6 at count 2, and at most -3.41 at every count>=3 (train). It forms the upper edge of the response: three or more active indicators always switch the output off. Evidence: closed form, plus per-count ranges on the train split (n=345).
ann_26.proposed: This part slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' when a1, a3, a5 or a6 moves away from its first value and slightly lowers it when a2 or a4 takes its first value; it also separates a2 = 2 from a2 = 3.

ann_27.original: Output = sigmoid(Ramp - 1.20 - 5.64*Gate): an additive composition under the output sigmoid. Unconnected inputs a2:2, a4:2, a4:3, a5:2, a5:3 and a5:4 are zero-effect entries; the model never consults them. When no indicator is active the gate is about 13, and its -5.64 readout overwhelms the ramp (logit about -54). With one active indicator the gate still wins (logit <= -8.96). With two, the gate is (almost) off and the logit equals the ramp, -3.34 to +5.63. With three or more, the ramp itself is <= -3.41. So the network produces a peak at count two of the six rule indicators. The ramp makes the upper edge and the gate makes the lower edge: the mirror image of a single gate plus ramp construction. Because the ramp weights are uneven, the peak is not level. Pairs involving a6=1 (with a1, a2, a4 or a5) get logits -3.34 to -1.07 and fall below p=0.5, and so do some a2&a4 and a4&a5 configurations; a3&a6 stays positive because I3 is light. Train evidence (n=345): AUC 1.0, since every count-2 logit (>= -3.337) exceeds every other logit (<= -3.408), a margin of only 0.07. Accuracy at 0.5 is 0.890: 38 false negatives, all count-2 rows, and no false positives. Local ablation with the gate set to 0 drops train accuracy to 0.632 and turns every count<=1 row positive.
ann_27.proposed: The model as a whole slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' when a2 changes from 3 to 2.

summary.text: The typical case has the most common value of each attribute (a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1); with a6 = 2 instead, moving a5 away from its first value, or changing a1 from 1 to 2, clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 2% to about 99%, while with a6 = 1 it stays below 1%.
For the typical case with a5 other than 1, changing a1 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 81%, while with a5 = 1 it stays below 1%.
One part of the model acts on 95 of the 345 training cases, and 6 of those 95 are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case this part acts on, which has no attribute at its first value, it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.
Changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case, which stays below 1%.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
